background.definition: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a rare and life-threatining thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, and organ ischemia linked to disseminated microvascular platelet rich-thrombi.

list.listitem: 3 per 1 million adults per year based on the Oklahoma TTP - HUS Registry.
One to 2 cases of documented ADAMTS-13-deficient TTP per 1,000,000 per year in the US.
The incidence of TTP is greater in women, during pregnancy, and in Blacks.
TTP is caused by the deficiency of the von Willebrand factor (vWF) cleaving metalloprotease, ADAMTS13.
Idiopathic TTP is usually caused by autoantibodies to ADAMTS 13
Congenital or hereditary TTP (cTTP, also called Upshaw-Schulman Syndrome) is caused by mutations in the ADAMTS13 gene which results in severe deficiency of ADAMTS13, or ineffective ADAMTS13.
Secondary TTP that may be seen in connective tissue diseases, pregnancy, HIV, pancreatitis and malignancy.
A systematic review of case reports and case series found no convincing evidence of medications as a cause of TTP.
ADAMTS 13 is a specific metalloprotease among the family of ADAMTS, which cleaves vWF multimers releasing adherent platelets.
An ADAMTS13 deficiency results in increased levels of ultra-large vWF multimers.
Spontaneous intravascular platelet aggregation and widespread microthrombi occur especially in microvasculature where shear stress is high.

Suspect TTP when a patient presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), severe thrombocytopenia with or without symptoms of organ involvement and without another clinically apparent etiology. A
Hemoglobin is usually < 10 mg/dL and thrombocytopenia < 30,000/microL C
Consider using the PLASMIC score to predict the likelihood of ADAMTS13 deficiency as it helps to estimate the pre-test probability of TTP. B

No hemolytic anemia; no evidence of microvascular thrombosis

list.listitem: TTP is clasically characterized by the pentad of fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, renal and neurological dysfunction. Unfortunately, this pentad is only found in less than 5% of patients with TTP.
Fever, neurologic involvement, and renal failure are often absent and are not necessary for the diagnosis.
Fever is seen in less than 30% of cases.
Neurologic features like headache, encephalopathy, stroke or TIA are seen in up to 78% of patients.
Signs of thrombocytopenia such as petechiae, purpura and hematuria are seen in up to 55% of patients.
Cardiac involvement can occur and is considered a bad prognostic sign.
Ultimately, there are no symptoms that are specific for TTP and laboratory analysis is necessary for diagnosis.
Initial tests should include a complete blood count with peripheral blood smear and reticulocyte count.

Additional tests are coagulation studies (PT/PTT), a complete metabolic panel, a serum LDH level, and a direct Coombs test. Coagulation studies are usually normal in TTP. LDH is usually elevated and a Coombs test is usually negative. Reticulocytosis is often present.
An HIV test and hepatitis serologies should be performed to search for alternative causes.

Confirmatory tests include ADAMTS 13 activity. This is usually <10% if the cause is idiopathic or congenital. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting results. Secondary causes of TTP have ADAMTS 13 activity that is variable. The risk of relapse for patients diagnosed with idiopathic TTP is greater with low ADAMTS 13 levels and a younger age at diagnosis.
ADAMTS 13 autoantibody (IgG) ELISA can also be used to confirm the autoimmune etiology in idiopathic TTP.
TTP is a clinical diagnosis.
Order CBC with peripheral smear and reticulocyte count, CMP, Coombs test, clotting profile and ADAMTS13 levels when diagnosis is suspected.

Secondary causes such as hypertensive emergency, malignancy, severe preeclampsia, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), HIV, Hepatitis B/C, pregnancy, and sepsis should be ruled out if clinical suspicion is high.
Sensitivity of ADAMTS 13 activity assays for the diagnosis of TTP (using a cutoff of <10% activity as abnormal) ranges from 89% to 100% with a specificity greater than 91%.
Treat TTP as a medical emergency and obtain urgent hematology consult. C
For suspected TTP initiate plasma exchange as soon as possible B
Give methylprednisolone or high dose oral prednisolone B
Consider rituximab as an adjunct to plasma exchange and corticosteroids. B
Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma) was recently approved for treatment of congenital TTP and is highly effective.B
See for a suggested overview of treatment. C

Glucocorticoids are recommended for all patients with TTP per the British Guidelines. In the US, in the absence of contraindication glucocorticoids are added as an adjunct to plasma exchange although the mode of administration is debatable.

For persons with congenital TTP, recombinant ADAMTS13 was highly effective at preventing thrombocytopenic episodes compared with standard therapy in a randomized trial with 48 patients. There were trends toward less abdominal pain and neurologic symptoms as well.

Rituximab has been used in cases refractory to plasma exchange and in relapsing cases of idiopathic TTP with significant success.. The precise recommendations on criteria to start it is being evaluated.
Cyclosporine has been used as an adjunct to plasma exchange as well as in refractory and relapsing cases.
Vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and azathioprine have been used with varying results.

There is a weak recommendation to initiate caplacizumab after confirmation of acute TTP and up to 30 days after completion of plasma exchange. A systematic review found some evidence that it is associated with lower rates of mortality and relapse, although increases bleeding risk.
Splenectomy can be used for patients with recurrent bouts or refractory idiopathic TTP.

In one case series, 6 of 6 patients with refractory TTP were discharged alive from the hospital free of disease. Among 8 patients with recurrent TTP, 4 had no further episodes and the other 4 had a reduction in frequency from 1.0 to 0.3 per year.
Plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma is first-line treatment. Plasma exchange has been shown to significantly decrease mortality in TTP compared with plasma infusion (RR 0.31; 95% CI, 0.21-0.79).

Standard guidelines are daily plasma exchange with replacement of 1.0 to 1.5 times the predicted plasma volume of the patient. The British guidelines recommend that plasma exchange be continued for 2 days after the platelet count returns to normal (>150,000 per cubic millimeter).
Plasma infusion should be performed when plasma exchange cannot be used or is delayed.
The risk of relapse for patients diagnosed with idiopathic TTP is greater with low ADAMTS-13 levels and a younger age at diagnosis. B
Male gender, severe thrombocytopenia (<13,000/mL), and high LDH are associated with relapse. B
Survival at 6 months is estimated at 78% with plasma exchange. A

There is a lack of good evidence for treatment in pregnancy. General recommendations include aspirin if platelets >50,000 per cubic millimeter. If platelets are <50,000 per cubic millimeter, aspirin is not recommended.
Low-molecular-weight heparin is used as preventative therapy for women with a history of TTP.

General recommendations, based upon expert opinion and case reports, are for plasma exchange at least every 2 weeks. In women who have had TTP during prior pregnancies, plasma exchange is recommended to commence as soon as possible. Prednisolone is often used in conjunction with plasma exchange with no additional harm reported.
Pregnant women with active TTP or TTP during prior pregnancies should be closely managed by a multidisciplinary team.
It is very unusual for anyone under the age of 20 to present with idiopathic TTP.
This must be distinguished from the diarrhea-related HUS typically seen in children. The treatment is supportive in HUS.

TTP in children is usually due to an inactivating mutation in the ADAMTS 13 gene. Symptoms may be apparent at birth or present later in life. Exacerbations are usually triggered by infections, surgery, or other stresses.
Plasma infusion, from 5 to 10 mL/kg of plasma every 2 to 3 weeks is usually sufficient.

algorithm.title: Suggested Approach to Management of an Initial Episode of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP).

cell.label: The patient has thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with no apparent cause. TTP is diagnosed.
Is the patient a young child with renal failure and a prodrome of diarrhea?
Begin plasma exchange. Add glucocorticoids if TTP appears to be idiopathic. Continue to search for an alternative cause, such as cancer or sepsis. Is an alternative cause discovered?
Continue treatment and follow the platelet count to measure response. Does the platelet count steadily increase to normal?

Add glucocorticoids, or if the patient is already receiving glucocorticoids, add more intensive immunosuppressive agents. Consider increasing the volume of plasma exchanged. When the platelet count exceeds 150,000/mm3 for 2 consecutive days, consider stopping plasma exchange gradually rather than abruptly. Does the platelet count remain normal?
Resume daily plasma exchange and intensify immunosuppressive treatment.

Maintain the central venous catheter until the risk of exacerbation decreases (1–3 wk) to avoid the risks associated with placement of a new catheter. Remission is achieved when the platelet count remains normal for 30 days after the discontinuation of plasma exchange.
Stop plasma exchange when the platelet count exceeds 150,000/mm3 for 2 consecutive days, then begin to taper glucocorticoids. Does the platelet count remain normal after plasma exchange is stopped?
Stop plasma exchange. Begin appropriate management.
Manage with supportive care and no plasma exchange.
